姆爾丹加鼓主要用於印度東北部與東部的虔誠音樂伴奏。阿薩姆地區見於宗教戲劇、歌樂、: The mrdanga is used mainly to accompany devotional music in north-east and eastern India. In Assam it appears in religious drama, song, narrative chant and lyric songs, and it accompanies Sattriya dance; it is also used in the arati ritual of Vishnu temples in Odisha, in Odia and Bengali kirtan, and in Gaudiya dance. ISKCON and Gaudiya Vaishnava groups use it as the main drum for bhajan and kirtan. Its two heads, one high and one low, give an accompaniment in which rhythm and bass alternate.
姆爾丹加鼓以雙手手掌與手指擊打兩面。右面較小，發高音；左面較大，發低音。初學時先: The mrdanga is struck on both heads with the palms and fingers of both hands. The right head is smaller and gives the high note; the left is larger and gives the bass. A beginner practises each head separately first, learning where the high and low strokes fall. If the bass is weak, a little water can be dabbed on the rim of the larger head and left for a few minutes, or the head stretched with the palm, to bring the note down.
姆爾丹加鼓傳統上為陶土製雙面鼓，鼓身中空，兩端蒙皮，其中一面明顯較小。鼓皮以牛皮: The mrdanga is traditionally a double-headed drum of clay, hollow, with skin at both ends, one of them clearly smaller. The heads are of cow or goat skin and are treated in three layers, with a coating of rice paste, glue and iron powder around the edge. Some modern instruments use a fibreglass shell and synthetic heads. The source does not state the materials of the other parts.
姆爾丹加鼓為兩面陶土鼓，右面較小，音高較高，帶有金屬感；左面較大，發較低之低音，: The mrdanga has two clay heads: the right is smaller and higher, with a metallic quality; the left is larger and gives a lower bass, and its range is the contrast between the two. Its pitch is affected by humidity: in damp weather the larger head slackens and vibrates more, giving a lower note, and in dry weather it tightens and the note rises. The player can dab water on the rim and let it stand, or stretch the head with the palm, to adjust the pitch of the larger head. 姆爾丹加鼓的起源有多種說法，其出自印度奧里薩、西孟加拉、阿薩姆與曼尼普爾，並在東: There are several accounts of the mrdanga's origin; it comes from Odisha, West Bengal, Assam and Manipur in India, and different forms developed in the north-east. The Assamese scholar Sankardev changed the wooden drum to clay and brought the drum into the song tradition, which made it an important percussion instrument in Ekasarana Dharma culture, in religious drama, narrative praise and lyric song. It also accompanies Odishan and Bengali praise singing and Gaudiya dance, and is used in the arati ritual of Vishnu temples and in the devotional singing and praise of ISKCON.

The mrdanga (Khol) is a double-headed clay membranophone used in north-east and eastern India, Hornbostel–Sachs 211.23. The shell is hollow, with heads at both ends, one larger and one smaller, traditionally of cow or goat skin and coated with a paste of rice, glue and iron powder; there are also fibreglass shells and synthetic heads. The player strikes it with the palms and fingers of both hands. It is often used in devotional music, in the offering ritual of Vishnu temples, in kirtan chanting, and in the religious drama, song and dance of Assam.
